e.t: This noun means “want of counsel” or “thoughtlessness.” It describes a condition in which a person lacks sound guidance or acts without careful judgment. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Proverbs and once in Baruch. Its central idea is not merely ignorance, but the absence of wise counsel or thoughtful decision-making. The surrounding verse determines how that condition is expressed in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “make wild”: it describes causing someone or something to become wild rather than tame or controlled. As a verb, it expresses an action or change, not a person, object, or quality by itself. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:2. The surrounding verse is not included here, so the exact subject and situation must be understood from that passage’s context.

Azōbai, also rendered “Azove,” is a personal name rather than a term describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:37, so its meaning is chiefly its identification of the named person. No additional descriptive sense or explanation of the name’s origin is provided here. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place within it.

This adjective means “spotless,” describing something free from stain, blemish, or defilement. It presents a condition of cleanness and purity rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom: Wisdom 4:9 and Wisdom 7:26. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains that of being unmarked by anything that would make it impure or flawed.

This Greek LXX noun means “threshing,” referring to the work of threshing harvested grain. It names an agricultural activity rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Leviticus 26:5 and once in Amos 9:13. Its basic sense remains focused on threshing, while the surrounding verse determines the specific promise, picture, or statement in which the activity appears.

This adjective describes someone or something as “unlucky” or “wretched.” It expresses an unfavorable or pitiable condition rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Song of Songs 2:5, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic sense points to a state marked by misfortune or distress, and it may describe a person or circumstance viewed as suffering under such a condition.

This verb means “go through,” describing movement through something or from one side to another. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Proverbs 9:12. The basic meaning is action-oriented: it presents someone as passing through rather than merely remaining in place. The surrounding verse supplies the specific setting and force, but the word itself contributes the idea of going through. Its precise sense in that verse should therefore be understood alongside the complete sentence and passage.

This verb means “rebuild”: to build something again after it has been damaged, destroyed, or removed. It describes renewed construction, whether of a physical structure or something represented as being built up again. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, it occurs 20 times across 19 verses, from Deuteronomy through Malachi. Its use in passages concerning Jerusalem, houses, and restoration keeps the central idea concrete: something that existed before is made firm or complete again. The precise force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage says is being rebuilt.

This verb means “hang,” describing the action of hanging someone or something. It expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 17:23, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word itself remains focused and direct: it identifies hanging as the action being expressed.

This verb means “reject”: to refuse, dismiss, or regard someone or something as unacceptable. It describes an active response rather than simple neglect. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, especially in Jeremiah, and is also found in Psalms, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its central idea remains the same wherever it appears: a person, people, or thing is refused rather than accepted. The surrounding verse determines what is being rejected and why.

This Greek LXX verb means to rave or rage with extreme intensity—to express uncontrolled, excessive anger or agitation. Its wording points to behavior that goes beyond ordinary irritation and reaches an uttermost degree. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Daniel 12:4. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself describes furious, unrestrained expression rather than quiet displeasure.

This noun refers to a “runaway slave,” and by extension describes “a deserter; rebel.” It identifies someone who has abandoned an obligation, allegiance, or place and is viewed as having turned away. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented by this LXX entity, the word occurs eight times. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is desertion or rebellion against an expected loyalty.

This Greek LXX adverb describes something as “lifted up” or situated “on high.” It points to an elevated position or upward direction rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Kings and once in Malachi. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains elevation—being raised upward or placed above.

This Greek LXX noun means “first leader; founder”—someone who begins something and stands at its head. It describes an originator or pioneering leader, emphasizing priority in beginning together with the responsibility of leading. The central idea is not simply holding an office, but being the one who initiates and directs something. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:30.

This noun means “ruling jailer”: the person who oversees or commands a prison and those held there. It refers to an official with authority over a jail, rather than simply any prisoner or guard. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 40:4. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to the jail’s governing officer.

Asir is a personal name, not a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named Asir. The name occurs four times in this corpus: once in Exodus and three times in 1 Chronicles. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning here is primarily identification rather than a broader concept or instruction.

Astarteion, also rendered Astartion, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 31:10. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine the entity’s exact nature or significance without the surrounding verse and passage.

Atara is a personal name, referring to a woman or person identified by that name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:26. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Atara itself.

This Greek LXX noun means “dismissal” or “forgiveness”: the release of a person, obligation, or offense. It can describe being sent away or freed, and it can describe the cancellation of guilt or debt. The word occurs 47 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, appearing especially often in Leviticus, where release from service, property obligations, and other claims is discussed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says is released.

e.h: A Proper Name: Baian or Vean
e.t: This word is a proper name, rendered “Baian” or “Vean.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Numbers 32:3 and once in 1 Maccabees 5:4. The supplied information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to determine which specific person or location it identifies in either passage.

Barad, also written Varath, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary descriptive word or action; it functions as a personal name. The name occurs seven times in seven verses in the LXX, appearing in Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and Job. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular person identified in each occurrence cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore the name itself: Barad or Varath.

Basōdia, also identified as Vasothia, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Septuagint. It is not presented here as a general description or action word, but as the name of a specific entity. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Nehemiah 3:6. The available lexical information identifies the name itself, while the reference locates its single occurrence; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the name’s particular role there.

Bēthazaria, also rendered Vithazaria, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identifying name, and the surrounding passage is needed to determine exactly whom or what it identifies. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:24. The name should remain distinct as an LXX form and should not be treated as a common noun or assigned a broader meaning than the supplied name itself supports.

Belion, also rendered “Vilion,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Bel and the Dragon 1:22. The available lexical meaning identifies it simply as the name “Bēlion; Vilion.” Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but the word itself functions as a personal or place name, not as a broader theological or descriptive term.

This Greek verb means “eat,” describing the act of consuming food. It is used for ordinary eating in the Greek Old Testament, including instructions about food and sacrificial meals. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming the food itself. The word occurs 41 times across 40 verses in this Greek Old Testament corpus, from Exodus through the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means to make a booming or humming noise. It describes producing a noticeable, resonant sound rather than silently speaking or acting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, all within the books of 1 Chronicles and Jeremiah. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is making the sound and how the surrounding passage presents it, but the central idea remains an audible humming or booming noise.

This Greek LXX verb means to “plunge” or “overwhelm”—to thrust something down into depth or cause it to be overcome. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:4. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the action emphasizes sinking, submerging, or overpowering in that specific passage.

This word means “treasurer,” a noun for a person responsible for money, valuable goods, or a treasury. It identifies an official serving in that financial role, rather than describing the goods themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 1:8. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to a person entrusted with overseeing valuable resources.

Gesam is a proper name—the personal name of an individual mentioned in the Greek Old Testament text of Nehemiah. It is rendered Gesam and does not function as a general word describing an object, action, or quality. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all within Nehemiah: once in chapter 2 and twice in chapter 6. Its exact significance in each passage comes from the surrounding verse context.

This word means “knowledge; knowing”: awareness or understanding of something. As a noun, it names what a person knows or the possession of understanding, rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs 73 times, showing that it is a recurring way to speak about knowledge across biblical wisdom and narrative writings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being known and how the surrounding sentence uses the word.

e.h: To Circle or Draw a Circle
e.t: This LXX verb means “circle” or “draw a circle.” It describes the action of making a rounded boundary or tracing something in a circular form. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Job and once in Sirach, showing the same basic action across both writings. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the act of circling or forming a circle.

This noun means “hide,” referring to the skin of an animal, especially as a physical material. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 24 times across 14 verses, with many occurrences in Exodus 26. The word can therefore describe hide as something counted, arranged, or used in a practical setting. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains animal hide or leather-like skin.

This Greek verb means to “diagnose” or “decide”: to examine something carefully and reach a judgment about it. It can describe discerning what is true or determining what should be done. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs eight times, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes careful discernment or the decision that follows.

This verb means “dissonant.” It describes dissonance as something expressed or occurring in a sentence, rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, each in a separate verse. Its basic sense remains focused on discord or lack of harmony, while the surrounding passage determines what is dissonant in a particular occurrence.

This adjective means “two-storied,” describing something built with two levels or floors. It identifies a physical structure by its vertical arrangement rather than by its materials, occupants, or purpose. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Genesis 6:16. Because the word is an adjective, it serves to describe a noun; the surrounding passage determines which structure is being described and how that detail functions there. Its basic meaning remains a straightforward description of something having two stories.

This verb means “knock”: to strike against something, usually at a door or other surface, so that an audible contact is made. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, it occurs once, in Judges 16:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its basic meaning remains the act of knocking or striking against something.

Egla is a personal name, used to identify a woman in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe a quality, action, or object; it functions as the person’s name. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, Egla occurs four times, all in the books of Numbers and Joshua. The name appears in Numbers 26:37, Numbers 27:1, Numbers 36:11, and Joshua 17:3. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identification, while the particular person’s role or circumstances must be understood from each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “move out of,” describing the action of departing from a place or position. It presents movement away from something rather than simply remaining or standing still. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Kings 6:11. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: leaving or moving away from a location or condition.

This word expresses moving away, being removed, or traveling a considerable distance. It functions as an adverb, describing how movement occurs rather than naming a person, object, or place. Its meaning can therefore be rendered as “remove” or “travel afar,” depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Judges 18:22 and Psalm 128:3. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on separation from something or movement to a distant place.

This adjective means “eleventh,” identifying someone or something that comes after the tenth in sequence. It is an ordinal word, so it marks position rather than quantity or identity. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material represented here, it occurs 21 times, describing an order, time, or numbered place. Its basic meaning remains straightforward wherever it appears: the person, object, or period is number eleven in its series.

This noun refers to apparel: clothing or garments worn by a person. It names what someone wears rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 11 times, showing a normal term for garments across several passages. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This verb means “shake in”: to move or jolt something inward or into a place. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing once in 2 Kings and four times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being shaken and where it is moved, but the central idea remains a forceful shaking inward or into something.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “stand out.” It describes something that is distinct, prominent, or noticeable in relation to what surrounds it. The word appears ten times across nine verses in the Greek Old Testament, including passages concerning physical structures and locations. Its basic idea remains focused on being set apart or projecting beyond the surrounding area, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the passage’s context.

This word means “backwards,” describing movement or direction toward the rear or behind. It functions as an adverb or preposition, so it can indicate where someone or something moves or is positioned. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, it occurs seven times. Its basic sense remains focused on looking or moving back rather than forward, though the surrounding sentence determines the precise direction being described.

This verb means “return”: to go back to a former place, person, or situation. In the Septuagint, it normally describes movement back or coming back again, rather than merely remaining where one is. It occurs nine times across nine Old Testament verses in the Greek Old Testament, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Job. The exact force in any verse depends on what or whom the subject returns to.

This Greek LXX noun means “plot”—a secret plan formed to bring about some purpose, often involving opposition or harm. It names the scheme itself rather than the person making it or the action of carrying it out. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including Esther and the Maccabean books. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a deliberate, concealed plan.

This adjective means “one-fifth of something.” It describes an amount equal to a fifth, functioning as a qualifier for whatever item, value, or portion is being discussed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, all within eight Old Testament verses, mostly in Leviticus and once in Numbers. Its central idea remains precise: it identifies an added or assessed amount as one part out of five, rather than naming the whole object or value itself.

This adjective means “equal,” describing something that matches another in measure, value, status, or comparison. It presents two things as alike rather than greater or lesser, though the exact aspect of equality depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach. Its recorded uses are in Sirach 9:10 and Sirach 31:27, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular comparison in either passage.

Erael, also known as Erel, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs one time, at 1 Chronicles 25:2. The name identifies a particular person in that passage, but the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, so that person’s specific role cannot be described responsibly. Its meaning is therefore best treated as a personal designation.

This word means “work.” It is a noun referring to work as an activity or task. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it is used broadly, including references to human labor, crafted work, and the works associated with God. It occurs 535 times in this LXX corpus, so its precise sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and subject. The central idea remains work: something undertaken, performed, or accomplished.

This word means “mirror”: a noun for an object that reflects a person’s appearance. Its ordinary meaning is concrete and straightforward. As a noun, it identifies the reflective object itself, not the act of looking or the image seen in it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and Sirach. The references are Wisdom 7:26 and Sirach 12:11, though the surrounding verse text is not available for explaining its particular use in either passage.

Esriel, also given as Ezril, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs four times in the LXX corpus, in Numbers, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.h: Hopeful and Full of Good Hope
e.t: This word describes someone or something hopeful—marked by good hope and a positive expectation. It can function as an adjective, describing a person or situation, and also as a noun referring to one characterized by hope. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times across Proverbs, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea is confident hopefulness rather than mere goodness or general approval.

This word means “hard.” It is a noun used to name or describe hardness—something firm, difficult, or not easily yielding. Its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its central idea is hardness rather than softness or ease. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 9:5. This is its normal lexical meaning within that corpus.

Zamarias is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:8. The available lexical meaning identifies the name simply as “Zamarias,” without providing an additional definition or explanation of its name meaning. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, which are not included here.

Ēlamar, also rendered Ilamar, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the personal name itself. In the Greek LXX text, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:31. The surrounding verse text is not provided here, so no further description of the person or his role can be stated from this word alone.

Thammuz is a proper name, referring to a figure or deity identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezekiel 8:14. The name itself identifies Thammuz rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this word-level entry establishes the name but does not explain the full significance of its appearance in Ezekiel.

Thekōin, also rendered Thekin, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or place, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs twice in the Greek text of Nehemiah, at Nehemiah 3:5 and Nehemiah 3:27. Its exact referent in either passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, since the name itself supplies identification rather than a descriptive meaning.

This adjective describes someone or something bold and spirited—showing confident energy, courage, or a forceful disposition. It can describe a person who acts with daring confidence, though the surrounding passage determines whether that boldness is admirable or reckless. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, this word occurs 11 times, including uses in Numbers, Proverbs, Sirach, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea is vigorous boldness rather than quiet restraint.

Iasouia is a proper name, represented in English as “Iasouia” or “Iasoia.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:36. The available information establishes the name’s identity and spelling, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain who or what it identifies there.

Iemoloch, also rendered Iemolokh, is a proper name referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, this name appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:34. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name itself does not provide further meaning beyond identifying the person named Iemoloch. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding context.

Iesebaal; Iesevaal is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:11. The available lexical information preserves the name in these two forms, so it should be understood as an identifying name rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. Its precise reference in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word denotes the number “20” and is identified with “resh.” It functions as a numeral rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:153. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included, its precise use there cannot be explained further; its lexical meaning remains the number twenty.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “guide.” It describes the action of directing someone or helping them follow a way. As a verb, it normally expresses something one person does for another person or group. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Job, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a camelopard, or giraffe—a tall, long-necked animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 14:5. The two supplied meaning terms identify the same animal, with “camelopard” being an older English name for a giraffe. The word therefore names a specific creature rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. Its precise role in Deuteronomy 14:5 depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This verb means to step down or descend—from a higher place to a lower one. It describes movement downward and is used broadly in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 304 times. The word can refer to physically going down, but the basic idea remains a change in direction from above to below. Its repeated use across many Old Testament books shows that it is an ordinary action word rather than a term limited to one special event or setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “flowing down.” It describes something characterized by movement or direction downward, with the emphasis on the downward flow itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 3:23. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise referent in that verse cannot be stated safely; its basic lexical sense remains a downward-flowing thing or feature.

This word refers to a register or enrollment: a recorded listing of people included in an organized group. It is an adjective, so it describes something connected with being entered on such a list rather than naming the list itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 31:18. Its basic sense points to recognized membership recorded for orderly administration, while the surrounding verse determines the precise thing being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “pull down”: it describes bringing something from a higher position to a lower one, or causing it to fall. As an action word, it focuses on the act of lowering or overturning rather than on the object itself. It occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament, across passages from 2 Samuel through Zechariah. The surrounding context determines whether the action is physical or concerns something being brought down figuratively.

This verb means “steal from”: to take something belonging to another person without permission. It describes the act of depriving someone of what is theirs, rather than merely referring to loss or absence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 31:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the action of stealing from another person.

This adjective means “hidden,” describing something kept out of sight, not openly seen, or concealed from ordinary view. It functions as a descriptive word, so its precise force depends on the person, thing, or place it modifies in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, appearing in Exodus, Jeremiah, Lamentations, and Wisdom. Its basic sense remains consistent: what is secret, unseen, or concealed rather than openly visible.

This noun means “glory” or “renown,” referring to honor, distinction, or celebrated standing. It describes the recognition associated with someone regarded as notable or esteemed. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 14:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains the honor or fame connected with glory. The word is distinct within the Greek Old Testament corpus and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament occurrence.

Kōlitas, also rendered Kolitas, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:23. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is chiefly identification: it distinguishes this person from others mentioned in the passage. The name itself does not provide a separate description or explanation of the person’s character or actions.

Lobena is a proper name, also represented as Lovena. It functions as a name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its basic lexical function is clear: it is a personal or place name preserved in the biblical text.

This Greek LXX verb means “make bald”: to remove or cause the hair on someone’s head to be absent. It describes an action that produces baldness rather than naming a person or condition. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 13:25. Its basic sense remains focused on making someone bald, while the surrounding verse determines the exact force of the action in that passage.

This word means “length”: the extent of something from one end or point to another. As a noun, it names a measurable span rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, including its deuterocanonical books, it occurs eight times, with four occurrences in Psalms. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording and immediate context.

Μεῖραξ is a noun meaning “young girl” or “lass.” It refers to a young female, describing her age and sex rather than naming a specific title, role, or spiritual quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees, at 14:6 and 14:8. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what the word describes in each passage.

Melchol is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 17 times across 16 verses, chiefly in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, and once in 1 Chronicles. The English rendering preserves the name as “Melchol,” also written “Melkhol” in the lexical definition. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identification of that individual; the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is happening whenever the name appears.

This verb means “interchange” or “exchange”: it describes one thing being changed for, traded with, or substituted by another. It is an action word, focusing on the act of making such a change rather than merely describing a different condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 11 times, appearing in Esther and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what people or things are being exchanged or changed.

This noun means “eating of unclean food.” It refers to the act or practice of consuming food regarded as unclean, rather than merely describing the food itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the consumption of food considered unclean.

This word refers to the intellect or mind—the inner faculty by which a person thinks, understands, and reasons. It is a noun describing a person’s mental capacity rather than an outward action or physical object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, including uses rendered “mind” and “intellect.” The precise force in any particular verse depends on its surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the thinking and understanding part of a person.

This Greek LXX noun means “building,” referring to something built or a constructed place. It is used eight times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, so its basic sense is consistent across several books rather than limited to one passage. The word appears in descriptions involving buildings or construction, but the precise significance in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entity.

This word refers to an instrument or organ, especially something used to produce music. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 27 times, including passages describing musical instruments used in worship and celebration. Its basic meaning remains broad enough to include an organ or another kind of instrument; the surrounding verse identifies the particular object intended.
